terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation: aliquid alicui concēdere
evidence: Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.7: nōn enim concēdō tibi plūs ut illum amēs quam ipse amō
Plaut. Cas. 2.3.47 (old numbering): illum mihi aequius est quam mē illī quae volō concēdere (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To grant something to someone, as a favour or from regard for them; in argument, to grant a point (concēdō, I grant that, with an accusative and infinitive). Its first sense is to go away, make way: Concēde hūc, move over here (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: verb phrase: dō, dare, dedī, datum, with the dative of the person
evidence: Verg. A. 4.435–436: extrēmam hanc ōrō veniam … quam mihi cum dederit
Lewis & Short s.v. venia: “most usual in the phrase veniam dare, to grant a favor”
terms.comment: Venia is indulgence, a favour; to ask one, veniam ōrāre, petere. It is also pardon: veniam dare can mean to forgive (see allow, give).

phrases.latin: nōn enim concēdō tibi plūs ut illum amēs quam ipse amō
phrases.english: for I don’t grant that you love him more than I do

phrases.latin: extrēmam hanc ōrō veniam (miserēre sorōris), quam mihi cum dederit cumulātam morte remittam
phrases.english: this last favour I beg (pity your sister): when he has granted it, I shall repay it in full with my death

sources: Lewis & Short: concedo · Lewis & Short: venia

Quotation from the Latinitas loci collection (loci-cicero-epistulae), checked against the editions named there. Vergil checked against the Latin Library texts (CLTK mirror) (11 November 2026); that edition reads dederit in 436, where others read dederis.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
